steps.title: The bakery sign
paragraphs: A bakery put up a new sign: “Fresh cookie’s and muffin’s daily!”
A girl walking by frowned. “Cookie’s what?” she asked her dad. “The cookie’s hat? The cookie’s homework?”
Her dad laughed. “They mean more than one cookie. That’s just cookies, no apostrophe.”
An apostrophe has only two jobs. Plurals isn’t one of them.

cards.title: Job 1: missing letters
cards.body: In a contraction, the apostrophe sits where letters were taken out: do not → don’t, I am → I’m, they are → they’re, we will → we’ll, it is → it’s. In formal essays, use contractions sparingly.

cards.title: Job 2: belonging
cards.text:
One owner: add ’s → the dog’s bowl, Sam’s bike, James’s coat
More than one owner ending in s: add ’ → the dogs’ bowls, the girls’ team
Plural not ending in s: add ’s → the children’s books, the men’s room
cards.note: First write the owner, then add the apostrophe. Owner “girls” → girls’. Owner “children” → children’s.

cards.title: The tricky pairs
cards.telling: Its raining and the dog lost it’s ball. Your late! Their coming.
cards.showing: It’s raining and the dog lost its ball. You’re late! They’re coming.
cards.note: Test: say it as two words. “It is raining” works → it’s. “The dog lost it is ball” doesn’t → its. The same goes for you’re/your and they’re/their.

cards.title: No apostrophe for plurals
cards.body: More than one is just s: cookies, apples, the 1990s, CDs. Possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe either: its, yours, hers, ours, theirs.

prompts: Which pair (its/it’s, your/you’re, their/they’re) do you mix up most? What trick will you use?
Explain the difference between “the girl’s team” and “the girls’ team”.
